newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Broker mergers, Acordia.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Broker mergers, Acordia.

text.p: A review of the 1996 results posted by international insurance brokers and the comments from chief executives and analysts points to a clear conclusion -- with times as tough as they are, acquisition is the best hope for growth in 1997.
The candidates for acquisition are running out, but the latest to emerge is the property casualty division of Acordia, the Indianapolis-based broker.

Acordia is the world's 7th largest broker and third largest in the U.S., but its property casualty business accounted for more than half its $661 million revenues in 1996, enough to make it the 12th largest in the world in its own right.

Anthem Insurance Companies Ltd, which owns 67 percent of Acordia, is reported in the U.S. insurance press to be keen on focusing on health care business, and it does not take a genius to work out that now is the best time to get a good price for selling a brokerage business.
Acordia is a middle-market commercial broker with a good reputation, although it lacks any of the niche specialisms so highly regarded these days.

Who might buy it? Of its U.S. rivals, most are either settling other mergers, have insufficient capital, or would be unlikely to view the deal as a good strategic fit. While a non-insurance player could move in, perhaps more likely is a company such as UK broker Sedgwick, which would appear to have the capital and could benefit from greater participation in the U.S. market, home of its major rivals.

Even Willis Corroon, unless some other development seals its fate, will have to look at all acquisition options, although it will more likely focus on smaller businesses. Anyway, its performance in the U.S. has been less than brilliant, and the company has recently offloaded several U.S. units.

As Proteus has pointed out, global reach is a main driving force in these developments, but shareholder opinion is also important. Shareholders want greater efficiency and economy of scale, and are particularly keen to prune the costs of brokerage when competition is so tight.

For some of the brokers which have expanded, it was seen as a means to keep adding value to shareholders. With the soft market and heavy competition, some would have shown flat results had it not been for their acquisitions. Others still find themselves in that position.
